The Jacobian Conjecture: Approximate roots and intersection numbers

Abstract.

We translate the results of Yansong Xu into the language of [6], obtaining nearly the same formulas for the intersection number of Jacobian pairs, but with an inequality instead of an equality.

Introduction

The Jacobian Conjecture (JC) in dimension two stated by Keller in [4] says that any pair of polynomials P,Q∈L≔K⁡[x,y]P,Q\in L\coloneqq K[x,y], with [P,Q]≔∂xP​∂yQ−∂xQ​∂yP∈K×[P,Q]\coloneqq\partial_{x}P\partial_{y}Q-\partial_{x}Q\partial_{y}P\in K^{\times}, defines an invertible automorphism of LL. If this conjecture is false, then we can find a counterexample such that the shape of the support of the components P≔f⁡(x)P\coloneqq f(x), Q≔f⁡(y)Q\coloneqq f(y), is contained in rectangles (0,0)(0,0), m⁡(a,0)m(a,0), m⁡(a,b)m(a,b), m⁡(0,b)m(0,b) and (0,0)(0,0), n⁡(a,0)n(a,0), n⁡(a,b)n(a,b), n⁡(0,b)n(0,b), such that m⁡(a,b)m(a,b) is in the support of PP and n⁡(a,b)n(a,b) is in the support of QQ. In a recent paper [8] Yangsong Xu gives two formulas for the intersection number of possible counterexamples, which we call IMI_{M} and ImI_{m}. If the formulas were true, we would be able to discard many infinite families of possible counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture described in [2].

When we translated the result and the proofs of [8] into the language of [6], we obtained the same formula for IMI_{M}, but for ImI_{m} we obtained only an inequality, consequently we cannot discard the infinite families as desired.

Hence, the main result of the present article is the translation of the concept of approximate roots into our language (see [6], also [3] and [2]), which requires a dictionary from Moh’s language to our language. It is interesting on its own, and the modified formulas could help understand some features of Moh’s methods.

Along this paper we will freely use the notations of [6].

2  Two formulas for the Intersection number

Recall that the intersection number of two bivariate polynomials PP and QQ is defined by I⁡(P,Q)≔degx⁡(Resy⁡(P,Q))I(P,Q)\coloneqq\deg_{x}({\Res_{y}}(P,Q)), where Resy⁡(P,Q){\Res_{y}(P,Q)} denotes the resultant of PP and QQ as polynomials in yy. In [8], the author defines for a Jacobian pair (P,Q)(P,Q) the polynomial Pξ≔P⁡(x,y)−ξP_{\xi}\coloneqq P(x,y)-\xi, where ξ\xi is a generic element of the field KK, and gives two different formulas for I⁡(Pξ,Q)I(P_{\xi},Q), one in terms of the major roots in [8]*Theorem 5.1 and the other in terms of the minor roots in [8]*Theorem 4.7. We will prove the first formula using our language in Theorem 3.15, and instead of the equality in the formula for ImI_{m} we will prove an inequality in Theorem 3.25. In order to do this, it will be convenient to provide a proof of the preparatory results of [8] in the language of [6].

We will first define approximate roots, final major roots and final minor roots using our language.

2.1  Approximate π\bm{\pi}-roots

In this section we will consider a polynomial P∈LP\in L, which is monic in yy. For l∈ℕl\in\mathds{N} we will consider the following algebras:

L=K[x,y]⊊K[x±1l,y]⊊K((x−1/l))[y]⊊K[π]((x−1/l))[y],L=K[x,y]\subsetneq K[x^{\pm\frac{1}{l}},y]\subsetneq K((x^{-1/l}))[y]\subsetneq K[\pi]((x^{-1/l}))[y],

where π\pi is a variable (“symbol” in [8]). We also will use the subring Lπ(l)≔K[π][x±1/l,y]L_{\pi}^{(l)}\coloneqq K[\pi][x^{\pm 1/l},y] of K[π]((x−1/l))[y]K[\pi]((x^{-1/l}))[y]. Note that degx=v1,0\deg_{x}=v_{1,0} is well defined in K[π]((x−1/l))[y]K[\pi]((x^{-1/l}))[y].

Unless otherwise indicated, we will consider the elements PP of the above mentioned algebras as polynomials in yy with coefficients in one of the algebras K⁡[x]K[x], K⁡[x±1l,y]K[x^{\pm\frac{1}{l}},y], K[π]((x−1/l))K[\pi]((x^{-1/l})),…. Consequently expressions like P⁡(τ)P(\tau), P⁡(α)P(\alpha),…, will denote PP with yy replaced by τ\tau, PP with yy replaced by α\alpha, etc.

By the Newton-Puiseux Theorem (see [1]*Corollary 13.15, page 295) there exist l∈ℕl\in\mathds{N} and αi,βi∈K((x−1/l))\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\in K((x^{-1/l})) such that

P=∏i=1M(y−αi).P=\prod_{i=1}^{M}(y-\alpha_{i}).

We set ℛ(P)={αi:i=1,…,M}\mathcal{R}(P)=\{\alpha_{i}:i=1,\dots,M\}.

Definition 2.1.

Let α∈ℛ⁡(P)\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P) and write α=∑jaj​xj\alpha=\sum_{j}a_{j}x^{j} with j∈1l​ℤj\in\frac{1}{l}\mathds{Z}. The π\pi-approximation of α\alpha up to xj0x^{j_{0}} is the element

τ≔∑j>j0aj​xj+π​xj0∈K⁡[π,x±1l].\tau\coloneqq\sum_{j>j_{0}}a_{j}x^{j}+\pi x^{j_{0}}\in K[\pi,x^{\pm\frac{1}{l}}].

Note that degx⁡(τ−α)=j0\deg_{x}(\tau-\alpha)=j_{0}.

Definition 2.2.

Let τ≔∑j>j0aj​xj+π​xj0∈K⁡[π,x±1l]\tau\coloneqq\sum_{j>j_{0}}a_{j}x^{j}+\pi x^{j_{0}}\in K[\pi,x^{\pm\frac{1}{l}}]. We set

DτP≔{α∈ℛ⁡(P):τ​ is the π-approximation of α up to xj0}.D_{\tau}^{P}\coloneqq\{\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P):\tau\text{ is the $\pi$-approximation of $\alpha$ up to $x^{j_{0}}$}\}.

We say that τ≔∑j>j0aj​xj+π​xj0∈K⁡[π,x±1l]\tau\coloneqq\sum_{j>j_{0}}a_{j}x^{j}+\pi x^{j_{0}}\in K[\pi,x^{\pm\frac{1}{l}}] is a π\pi-root of PP if there exists α∈ℛ⁡(P)\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P) such that π\pi approximates α\alpha up to xj0x^{j_{0}}. We say that j0j_{0} is the order of τ\tau.

Corollary 2.10.

Let τ≔∑j=1kaj​xj+π​xj0\tau\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_{j}x^{j}+\pi x^{j_{0}} be a π\pi-root of PP and let λ∈K\lambda\in K. 3  Approximate roots for Jacobian pairs

For the rest of the section we let (P0,Q0)(P_{0},Q_{0}) denote a Jacobian pair in LL satisfying the conditions required in [6]*Corollary 5.21, which in particular means that (P0,Q0)(P_{0},Q_{0}) is a minimal pair and a standard (m,n)(m,n)-pair for some coprime integers m,n>1m,n>1. By [6]*Proposition 4.6(3), there exist a<ba<b in ℕ\mathds{N} such that en1,0⁡(P0)=m⁡(a,b)\en_{1,0}(P_{0})=m(a,b) and en1,0⁡(Q0)=n⁡(a,b)\en_{1,0}(Q_{0})=n(a,b). So, by [6]*Corollary 5.21(4), we know that ℓ1,1​(P0)=λ​xa​m​yb​m\ell_{1,1}(P_{0})=\lambda x^{am}y^{bm} and ℓ1,1​(Q0)=λ′​xa​n​yb​n\ell_{1,1}(Q_{0})=\lambda^{\prime}x^{an}y^{bn} for some λ,λ′∈K×\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in K^{\times}. Replacing P0P_{0} by 1λ​P0\frac{1}{\lambda}P_{0} and Q0Q_{0} by 1λ′​Q0\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}Q_{0}, we can assume that λ=λ′=1\lambda=\lambda^{\prime}=1. Let ψ\psi be the automorphism of LL defined by ψ⁡(y)≔y\psi(y)\coloneqq y and ψ⁡(x)≔x+y\psi(x)\coloneqq x+y, and set P≔ψ⁡(P0)P\coloneqq\psi(P_{0}) and Q≔ψ⁡(Q0)Q\coloneqq\psi(Q_{0}) (see Figure 1). Since ψ\psi is (1,1)(1,1)-homogeneous,

(3.11) ℓ1,1​(P)=ψ⁡(ℓ1,1​(P0))=(x+y)m​a​ym​bandℓ1,1​(Q)=ψ⁡(ℓ1,1​(Q0))=(x+y)n​a​yn​b.\ell_{1,1}(P)=\psi(\ell_{1,1}(P_{0}))=(x+y)^{ma}y^{mb}\quad\text{and}\quad\ell_{1,1}(Q)=\psi(\ell_{1,1}(Q_{0}))=(x+y)^{na}y^{nb}.

Hence, PP and QQ are monic polynomials in yy and moreover, a straightforward computation shows that

(3.12) en1,0⁡(P)=m⁡(a,b)anden1,0⁡(Q)=m⁡(a,b).\en_{1,0}(P)=m(a,b)\quad\text{and}\quad\en_{1,0}(Q)=m(a,b).
Remark 3.1.

In the sequel we will establish several results about PP, but, since by [6]*Proposition 4.6 we know that (Q,P)(Q,P) is an (n,m)(n,m)-pair, the same results are valid mutatis mutandis for QQ.

Proposition 3.2.

Let α∈ℛ⁡(P)\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P) and let τ\tau be the π\pi-approximation of α\alpha up to xj0x^{j_{0}}. Assume that λτ≔degx⁡(P⁡(τ))>0\lambda_{\tau}\coloneqq\deg_{x}(P(\tau))>0, and take φ\varphi and (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) as in Proposition 2.6. The following facts hold:

  1. (1)

3.2  Intersection number and major roots

Lemma 3.14.

Let τ\tau be a final π\pi-root of PP. Then λτQ≔degx⁡(Q⁡(τ))=degx⁡(Q⁡(α))\lambda_{\tau}^{Q}\coloneqq\deg_{x}(Q(\tau))=\deg_{x}(Q(\alpha)) for α∈DτP\alpha\in D_{\tau}^{P}.

Proof.

We assert that fP,τ​(z)f_{P,\tau}(z) and fQ,τ​(z)f_{Q,\tau}(z) have no common roots. In fact, assume on the contrary that z−λz-\lambda is a common factor. If τ\tau is a major final root, then

a contradiction; whereas, if τ\tau is a minor root, then the choice of ξ\xi guarantees that fP,τf_{P,\tau} and fQ,τf_{Q,\tau} have no common roots.

3.3  Intersection number and minor roots

For the sake of brevity in the sequel we write PxP_{x}, QxQ_{x}, PyP_{y} and QyQ_{y} instead of the partial derivatives ∂xP\partial_{x}P, ∂xQ\partial_{x}Q, ∂yP\partial_{y}P and ∂yQ\partial_{y}Q, respectively.

Lemma 3.23.

Let (P,Q)(P,Q) be as above, (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) be a direction with ρ≠0\rho\neq 0 and α∈ℛ⁡(P)\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P). Write ℓρ,σ​(P)=xu​g​(z)\ell_{\rho,\sigma}(P)=x^{u}g(z) with z≔x−σ/ρyz\coloneqq x^{-\sigma/\rho}y. The following facts hold:

  2. (2)

    α\alpha is a minor root if and only if degx⁡(Q⁡(α))=0\deg_{x}(Q(\alpha))=0.

  3. (3)

    Let β∈ℛ⁡(Py)\beta\in\mathcal{R}(P_{y}). There exists τ∈Pm\tau\in P_{m} such that β∈DτPy\beta\in D_{\tau}^{P_{y}} if and only if degx⁡(P⁡(β))=0\deg_{x}(P(\beta))=0.

  4. (4)

    If α\alpha is a minor root, then degx⁡(Py​(α))=−δα\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha))=-\delta_{\alpha}.

  5. (5)

    Let τ∈Pm\tau\in P_{m} and assume that fPy,τf_{P_{y},\tau} and fQy,τf_{Q_{y},\tau} are coprime. Then degx⁡(Qy​(β))=−δτ\deg_{x}(Q_{y}(\beta))=-\delta_{\tau} for all β∈DτPy\beta\in D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}.

  6. (6)

    Let τ∈Pm\tau\in P_{m} and assume that fPy,τf_{P_{y},\tau} and fQy,τf_{Q_{y},\tau} are not coprime. Then there exists β∈DτPy\beta\in D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}, such that degx⁡(Qy​(β))<−δτ\deg_{x}(Q_{y}(\beta))<-\delta_{\tau}.

Proof.

(1) This follows from the fact that the morphism ∂y\partial_{y} satisfies ∂y(xi​yj)=j​xi​yj−1\partial_{y}(x^{i}y^{j})=jx^{i}y^{j-1} for j>0j>0, and so

vρ,σ​(∂y(xi​yj))=vρ,σ​(xi​yj)−σ.v_{\rho,\sigma}(\partial_{y}(x^{i}y^{j}))=v_{\rho,\sigma}(x^{i}y^{j})-\sigma.

Hence ℓρ,σ​(∂yP)=∂yℓρ,σ​(P)\ell_{\rho,\sigma}(\partial_{y}P)=\partial_{y}\ell_{\rho,\sigma}(P) when ∂yℓρ,σ​(P)≠0\partial_{y}\ell_{\rho,\sigma}(P)\neq 0, and so

ℓρ,σ​(Py)=∂y(xu​g​(z))=xu−σ/ρ​g′​(z),\ell_{\rho,\sigma}(P_{y})=\partial_{y}(x^{u}g(z))=x^{u-\sigma/\rho}g^{\prime}(z),

because deg⁡(g)>0\deg(g)>0.

(2) By items (1)a) and (2)c) of Proposition 3.13, we know that α\alpha is a minor root if and only if λτQ=0\lambda_{\tau}^{Q}=0 for the π\pi-root τ\tau associated to α\alpha. This proves (2), since λτQ=degx⁡(Q⁡(α))\lambda_{\tau}^{Q}=\deg_{x}(Q(\alpha)) by Lemma 3.14.

(3) Define

δβ≔min⁡{degx⁡(α−β)|α∈ℛ⁡(P)}.\delta_{\beta}\coloneqq\min\{\deg_{x}(\alpha-\beta)|\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P)\}.

Write

β=∑j>δβaj​xj+λ​xδβ+∑j<δβaj​xj\beta=\sum_{j>\delta_{\beta}}a_{j}x^{j}+\lambda x^{\delta_{\beta}}+\sum_{j<\delta_{\beta}}a_{j}x^{j}

Then τ≔∑j>δβaj​xj+π​xδβ\tau\coloneqq\sum_{j>\delta_{\beta}}a_{j}x^{j}+\pi x^{\delta_{\beta}} is a π\pi-root of PP. Since 0<|DτPy|=|DτP|−10<|D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}|=|D_{\tau}^{P}|-1, by Remark 3.6 we know that λτP≥0\lambda_{\tau}^{P}\geq 0. Take α∈DτP\alpha\in D_{\tau}^{P} and let τ1\tau_{1} be the final π\pi-root of PP associated with α\alpha. Theorem 3.25.

Set Im=1−∑τ∈Pm(δτ+1)I_{m}=1-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}(\delta_{\tau}+1). Then Im≤I⁡(P,Q)I_{m}\leq I(P,Q). We also have

(3.15) I⁡(P,Py​Q)=deg⁡(P)−∑τ∈Pm|DτP|​(1+δτ).I(P,P_{y}Q)=\deg(P)-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P}|(1+\delta_{\tau}).
Proof.

It suffices to prove (3.15) and

(3.16) I⁡(P,Py)≤deg⁡(P)−1−∑τ∈Pm(|DτP|−1)​(δτ+1).I(P,P_{y})\leq\deg(P)-1-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}(|D_{\tau}^{P}|-1)(\delta_{\tau}+1).

In fact, equalities (3.15) and (3.16) yield

I⁡(P,Q)=I⁡(P,Py​Q)−I⁡(P,Py)=1−∑τ∈Pm(δτ+1),I(P,Q)=I(P,P_{y}Q)-I(P,P_{y})=1-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}(\delta_{\tau}+1),

as desired.

Proof of equality (3.15). By Lemma 3.24, for each α∈ℛ⁡(P)\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P) we have Py​(α)​dd​x​Q​(α)∈K×P_{y}(\alpha)\frac{d}{dx}Q(\alpha)\in K^{\times}. Moreover, by Lemma 3.23(2), if α\alpha is a major root, then degx⁡(Py​(α)​Q​(α))=1\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha)Q(\alpha))=1. On the other hand, if α\alpha is a minor root, then by Proposition 3.13(1)a), Lemma 3.14 and Lemma 3.23(4), we have

degx⁡(Py​(α)​Q​(α))=degx⁡(Py​(α))=−δα=−δτ,\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha)Q(\alpha))=\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha))=-\delta_{\alpha}=-\delta_{\tau},

where τ\tau is the minor final π\pi-root associated with α\alpha. Using this facts we obtain

I⁡(P,Py​Q)\displaystyle I(P,P_{y}Q) =∑α∈ℛ⁡(P)degx⁡(Py​(α)​Q​(α))\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal{R}(P)}\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha)Q(\alpha))
=∑τ∈Pm∑α∈DτPdegx⁡(Py​(α)​Q​(α))+∑τ∈PM∑α∈DτPdegx⁡(Py​(α)​Q​(α))\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}\sum_{\alpha\in D_{\tau}^{P}}\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha)Q(\alpha))+\sum_{\tau\in P_{M}}\sum_{\alpha\in D_{\tau}^{P}}\deg_{x}(P_{y}(\alpha)Q(\alpha))
=∑τ∈Pm|DτP|​(−δτ)+∑τ∈PM|DτP|+∑τ∈Pm|DτP|−∑τ∈Pm|DτP|\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P}|(-\delta_{\tau})+\sum_{\tau\in P_{M}}|D_{\tau}^{P}|+\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P}|-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P}|
=deg⁡(P)−∑τ∈Pm|DτP|​(1+δτ),\displaystyle=\deg(P)-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P}|(1+\delta_{\tau}),

where the first equality is obtained as in the proof of Theorem 3.15.

Proof of inequality (3.16). By Lemma 3.24, for each β∈ℛ⁡(Py)\beta\in\mathcal{R}(P_{y}), we have Qy​(β)​dd​x​P​(β)∈K×Q_{y}(\beta)\frac{d}{dx}P(\beta)\in K^{\times}. Define

Py,m≔{β∈ℛ⁡(Py): there exists a minor final π-root τ of P, such that β∈DτPy}.P_{y,m}\coloneqq\{\beta\in\mathcal{R}(P_{y}):\text{ there exists a minor final $\pi$-root $\tau$ of $P$, such that $\beta\in D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}$}\}.

Then, by Lemma 3.23(3), if β\beta is not in Py,mP_{y,m}, then degx⁡(Qy​(β)​P​(β))=1\deg_{x}(Q_{y}(\beta)P(\beta))=1. On the other hand, if β\beta is in Py,mP_{y,m}, then by items (3), (5) and (6) of Lemma 3.23, we have

degx⁡(P⁡(β)​Qy​(β))=degx⁡(Qy​(β))≤−δτ,\deg_{x}(P(\beta)Q_{y}(\beta))=\deg_{x}(Q_{y}(\beta))\leq-\delta_{\tau},

where τ\tau is the minor final π\pi-root associated with β\beta. Using this facts we obtain

(3.17) I⁡(Py,P​Qy)\displaystyle I(P_{y},PQ_{y}) =∑β∈ℛ⁡(Py)degx⁡(P⁡(β)​Qy​(β))\displaystyle=\sum_{\beta\in\mathcal{R}(P_{y})}\deg_{x}(P(\beta)Q_{y}(\beta))
=∑τ∈Pm∑β∈DτPydegx⁡(P⁡(β)​Qy​(β))+∑β∉Py,mdegx⁡(P⁡(β)​Qy​(β))\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}\sum_{\beta\in D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}}\deg_{x}(P(\beta)Q_{y}(\beta))+\sum_{\beta\notin P_{y,m}}\deg_{x}(P(\beta)Q_{y}(\beta))
≤∑τ∈Pm|DτPy|​(−δτ)+deg⁡(Py)−∑τ∈Pm|DτPy|\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}|(-\delta_{\tau})+\deg(P_{y})-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}|
=deg⁡(P)−1−∑τ∈Pm|DτPy|​(1+δτ)\displaystyle=\deg(P)-1-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}|D_{\tau}^{P_{y}}|(1+\delta_{\tau})
=deg⁡(P)−1−∑τ∈Pm(|DτP|−1)​(1+δτ).\displaystyle=\deg(P)-1-\sum_{\tau\in P_{m}}(|D_{\tau}^{P}|-1)(1+\delta_{\tau}).

Since, by the Jacobian condition,

Resy⁡(Py,Qy)​Resy⁡(Py,Px)=Resy⁡(Py,Qy​Px)=∏β∈ℛ⁡(Py)Qy​(β)​Px​(β)=1,\Res_{y}(P_{y},Q_{y})\Res_{y}(P_{y},P_{x})=\Res_{y}(P_{y},Q_{y}P_{x})=\prod_{\beta\in\mathcal{R}(P_{y})}Q_{y}(\beta)P_{x}(\beta)=1,

we have I⁡(Py,Qy)=0I(P_{y},Q_{y})=0, and so (3.17) yields inequality (3.16). ∎
